findings.reason: an implementer following the text adds a dead `request` arm while the real pre-worker phases (`held`, `awaiting-upstream`, `blocked-upstream`) are unlisted, so the exclusion set the whole mechanism turns on is wrong.
findings.text: §5 says the launch-side view keeps a same-run pointer "unless its phase is still pre-worker (`queued` or `request`)", but no pointer phase `request` exists: the phase vocabulary is `queued`/`held`/`awaiting-upstream`/`blocked-upstream` (WAITING_REQUEST_PHASES, reckon/crew/node.py:1569) and `starting`/`launching`/`launcher`/`dispatching` (_UNLAUNCHED_CLAIM_PHASES, reckon/crew/dispatch_claims.py:120); "request" is a wait-ref kind (`wait_ref_kind`, reckon/crew/queue_admission.py:2764), not a phase, and a literal reading writes a branch that can never fire

findings.reason: the unexercised arm is the one that prevents the repair from turning into a permanent launch refusal, and no stated case would fail if it were wrong.
findings.text: the done-when has one case with a `working` pointer (must refuse) and one with a `queued` pointer (must proceed), but no case where a same-run pointer names the tree with a dead worker, which is the arm that keeps a legitimate retry of a failed launch working; an implementation that treats every same-run pointer as a claim passes both stated cases and blocks every relaunch of a node

findings.reason: the summary is the plan's headline statement of what it fixes and now asserts, as its second promise, a cause the plan itself disproves.
findings.text: the plan summary still reads "a drop never trashes a live worktree", the premise §5 explicitly corrects (the drop was not involved; the successor's own second launch moved its tree), and it names none of §5's promise

findings.reason: the plan now carries two incompatible accounts of the same incident, and a reader entering at §1 would investigate a restore and a predecessor drop that do not exist.
findings.text: §1's second bullet still states that "a dropped request's cleanup trashed a live successor's worktree" and that "at 23:50Z a different inode was restored at the same path", both of which §5 and the cited investigation refute (no restore; 23:50 was local time for 22:50:26Z; the mover was the successor's own second launch)

findings.reason: the plan figure weights the fleet progress rollup and the roadmap's remaining-hours estimate, and adding a one-hour section without moving it silently drops an hour of estimated work.
findings.text: `plan-effort-hours` remains 3.0 while the section hours now sum to 4.0 (0.25 + 0.75 + 1.0 + 1.0 + the new §5 at 1.0), so the plan understates its own cost

findings.reason: §3 is declared `done` on a done-when whose named artifact resolves nowhere, so the plan's own evidence trail cannot be followed from the section that owns it.
findings.text: §3's done-when names `docs/evidence/fragments/a-queued-request-is-checked-when-queued/what-trashed-the-live-worktree.html`, which does not exist (`docs/evidence/fragments/a-queued-request-is-checked-when-queued/` is absent from the tree); the investigation note was actually written to `~/.config/reckon/crew/reports/reckon/what-trashed-the-live-worktree.md`, which is what §5 cites

findings.reason: the incident's caller is settled by the independent fact that gc empties a path and never creates one, so the overstated discriminator does not move the repair.
findings.text: §5 says the trash directory carried the tree name "which only that path produces", but the investigation's own caller table shows the three gc call sites pass no `run_id` either, so their trash names would also carry the tree name
